findings.lens: Presbyterian / Reformed (Westminster Standards, Three Forms of Unity)
findings.claim: Closing the Spirit history with '2013: Strange Fire conference restates the cessationist case' makes the most combative event the last word for our side, while the continuationist entries are all movements and renewals.
findings.evidence: The standard scholarly marker for the late-20th-century debate is Grudem (ed.), Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? Four Views (1996), where Gaffin (cessationist), Saucy (open but cautious), Storms and Oss set out the cases side by side.
findings.fix: { "when": "1996", "what": "Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? sets the cessationist (Gaffin), open-but-cautious (Saucy), and continuationist (Storms, Oss) cases side by side." }

findings.lens: Reformed charismatic (John Piper, Wayne Grudem, Sam Storms, Sovereign Grace Churches, Acts 29 continuationists)
findings.claim: The Spirit history has no entry for the third wave, the movement that produced every Reformed continuationist the quiz cites, so continuationism reaches the reader as Azusa plus mainline/Catholic renewal, always non-Reformed.
findings.evidence: Wagner coined 'third wave' in 1983 for Wimber's Vineyard and evangelicals embracing the gifts without Pentecostal second-blessing theology; Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy in the New Testament and Today (1988); Piper's 1990-91 sermons on gifts; Sovereign Grace (PDI, 1982) and Newfrontiers; Grudem ed., Are Miraculous Gifts for Today? (1996). The axis's own read-more (Grudem, Storms) belongs to this stream, which the history never mentions.
findings.fix: Insert before the 2013 entry: {"when": "1980s-90s", "what": "The 'third wave' (Wimber's Vineyard; Grudem, Storms, Piper) brings the gifts into Reformed and evangelical churches without Pentecostal second-blessing theology."}
